420-D04-AB Conformity Assessment - Day 5

Conformity assessment methodologies

Audit methods, tests, checklists aligned to frameworks, risk analysis and scheduling - assembled into the Lab 2 Part B conformity assessment plan for the fictional retailer Erable Cycles inc.

Learning objectives

By the end of the morning you can:

  1. Name the six audit methods and choose the method that fits the wording of a requirement.
  2. Build a reproducible sample and document the reason of each selected item.
  3. Define a test with its requirement, method, sample, measurable pass rule and evidence.
  4. Select 12-15 checklist items with written rules and map them to CIS (Center for Internet Security) Controls v8.1, ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001:2022, PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) v4.0.1 and NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0.
  5. Rate a finding with the 3x3 likelihood x impact matrix and justify the rating.
  6. Schedule the assessment on Days 7-10 within the case constraints, after a signed mandate.
  7. Assemble the six sections of the Lab 2 Part B assessment plan.

Recall of Day 4 - asset inventory and classification

About 15 minutes - links Day 4 to today
  • Twelve inventory columns in three groups: identification (1 Asset ID, 2 Name, 3 Type, 4 Owner, 5 Custodian, 6 Location/hosting, 7 Environment), classification (8 Sensitivity, 9 Flags, 10 Business impact C/I/A (confidentiality, integrity, availability)), maintenance (11 Dependencies, 12 Last review).
  • Owner = business manager accountable for the asset; custodian = the person or provider who operates and protects it. Two frequent mistakes: IT (information technology) as owner of everything, and supplier services without an owner. An empty owner cell is a finding.
  • Four sensitivity levels (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted) and two flags (PI (personal information), CHD (cardholder data)). Decision table in order: card number? credentials, keys or security configuration? personal information? published? otherwise Internal.
  • Frameworks that require an inventory: CIS (Center for Internet Security) Safeguards 1.1, 2.1, 3.2 - ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001:2022 A.5.9, A.5.12 - NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 ID.AM - PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) 12.5.1 and 9.5.1.1.
  • SPOF (single point of failure): the payment provider is critical because it supports online and in-store sales and there is only one.
  • Keeping the inventory current: review every 90 days and after each change; drift = a change without a ticket; reconcile in both directions.
  • Link to today: the 5 critical assets + the 2 VMs (virtual machines) become the scope of the assessment plan (Lab 2 Part B).

Lesson 1 - Audit methods and techniques

About 10 minutes - course plan topic: Audit methods and techniques (e.g., sampling, walkthroughs, observations)

1.1 From criteria to evidence to findings

An audit is a systematic, independent and documented process for obtaining objective evidence and evaluating it to determine to what extent the audit criteria are met. The audit criteria are the requirements used as the reference: in this course, the laws, contracts, standards and policies listed in your Lab 1 applicability register. Audit evidence is information that is verifiable and relevant to a criterion - a configuration output, a signed record, a log extract, a statement confirmed by a document.

An audit method is the defined way the auditor collects that evidence. The auditor then compares the evidence with the criterion; the result is an audit finding: a conformity, a nonconformity (a requirement is not met) or an observation (a weakness that is not yet a nonconformity). Every finding must be traceable to its evidence; a finding without evidence is only an opinion.

1.2 The six methods used in this course

Each method answers a different question. Document review answers "what is supposed to happen?"; interview answers "what do the people say happens?"; walkthrough and observation answer "what happens in practice?"; re-performance answers "does the control give the expected result when the auditor executes it?"; sampling answers "which part of the population was checked, and why those items?".

MethodWhat the auditor doesEvidence producedErable Cycles example (fictional)
Document reviewReads policies, procedures and recordsDocument or record extractThe Patch Management Procedure: is it approved and dated?
InterviewAsks the people who perform the activityInterview notesThe IT (information technology) Administrator explains how critical patches are approved
WalkthroughFollows one real case from start to end with the person who performs itNotes and the documents of that caseOne new-employee request, from the HR (Human Resources) form to the AD (Active Directory) account
ObservationWatches an activity or a setting as it happensObservation notes, screenshotThe nightly backup job starts and ends successfully
SamplingTests a subset of a population with a stated ruleSample list with the reason of each pick10 of the 45 laptops checked for patch level
Re-performance (technical test)Runs the check or the tool personallyTool or script outputGet-HotFix run by the auditor on LAB-WIN11

1.3 Three references, one vocabulary

Three widely used references describe the same methods with slightly different words. NIST SP 800-53A Rev. 5 defines three assessment methods - examine (documents, configurations, records), interview (people) and test (exercising a mechanism) - with two attributes: depth (basic, focused or comprehensive rigour) and coverage (how many and which objects are assessed). Release 5.2.0 of SP (Special Publication) 800-53A was published on August 27, 2025.

The testing procedures of PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) v4.0.1 (PCI SSC document library) use the verbs examine, observe and interview. ISO 19011:2026, the fourth edition of the guidelines for auditing management systems, published in May 2026 to replace the 2018 edition, describes document review, interviews, observation and sampling; it adds a defined term for remote auditing methods (video calls, screen sharing, shared document stores) and expands their guidance.

1.4 Sampling: population, sample and selection rule

The population is the complete set of items a requirement applies to (the 45 laptops). The sample is the part that is actually tested; one item is a sampling unit. In judgement-based sampling, the auditor selects items with knowledge of risk - for example the laptops with administrator rights. It is efficient, but its result cannot be generalized statistically to the population. In statistical sampling, every item has a known chance of selection (random selection), so the result can be extended to the population with a measured confidence.

A sampling plan records the population, the method, the size, the selection rule and the reason of every pick. A random generator started with a fixed seed gives the same picks every time, so another auditor can verify the selection. Sampling risk is the risk that the conclusion drawn from the sample differs from the conclusion that testing the full population would give. PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) v4.x states the rule for its assessments: the assessor either tests 100 % of the population or follows a defined sampling methodology, and a sample must cover every variant of the population and be large enough to give confidence that the controls are implemented across the whole population (PCI SSC FAQ on sampling; PCI DSS v4.x section "Sampling for PCI DSS Assessments").

1.5 Evidence quality and corroboration

Good evidence is sufficient (enough to support the conclusion), reliable (trustworthy) and relevant (linked to the criterion being tested). As a general rule, reliability increases when the evidence comes from an independent source, is an original rather than a copy, is generated by the system rather than typed by a person, and is obtained directly by the auditor. Evidence produced by re-performance is therefore stronger than a statement made in an interview.

Corroboration means confirming one source with a second, independent source: the IT (information technology) Administrator says that the firewall is on (interview) and the auditor runs Get-NetFirewallProfile (test). The audit life cycle described in ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 19011 runs in six stages: initiate, prepare, conduct, report, complete, follow up. Today's plan is the prepare stage; Lab 3 is conduct; the Project is report and follow up.

Key terms to learn - Lesson 1

Audit criteria
The requirements used as the reference of the audit (laws, contracts, standards, policies).
Audit evidence
Verifiable information relevant to a criterion (records, configurations, confirmed statements).
Audit finding
The result of comparing evidence with a criterion: conformity, nonconformity or observation.
Walkthrough
Following one real case from start to end with the person who performs it.
Re-performance
The auditor executes the check or the tool personally and compares the result.
Population / sample
All items a requirement applies to / the items actually tested.
Judgement-based sampling
Selection by the auditor using knowledge of risk; not statistically generalizable.
Statistical sampling
Random selection with a known probability; the result can be generalized with a measured confidence.
Sampling risk
Risk that the sample leads to a different conclusion than testing 100 % of the population.
Corroboration
Confirming one evidence source with a second, independent source.
Depth and coverage
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-53A attributes: rigour of a method, and how many objects are assessed.

Think about it

  • Which method would you use first to check that backups run every night, and which method would corroborate it?
  • Why is an interview alone not enough to conclude that the firewall is enabled?

Real-life example 1

Choosing which laptops to test: a reproducible sampling plan for MC-03

TaskSelect 10 of the 45 Windows 11 laptops for checklist item MC-03 (operating-system patch level), with written reasons and a reproducible random part.
Relation to the lectureApplies the two sampling families of section 1.4 - judgement-based picks (risk) and statistical picks (random with a seed) - and documents the selection, as section 1.5 requires.
Future labsLab 2 Part B step 4 (the sample column of your checklist), Lab 3 Part B on Day 8 (patch status) and Project section 5 (methodology).

Requirement MC-03 applies to the 45 laptops of Erable Cycles. Testing 45 laptops by hand does not fit in the time of Lab 3, so the plan tests a sample of 10. The auditor first applies two judgement criteria: J1 - the 3 laptops with local administrator rights, because a compromise of these laptops has a higher impact; J2 - one laptop per site, the one with the oldest security update, so that every type of location is represented and the laptops most likely to fail are included. The remaining 5 laptops are drawn at random with the seed 20261107 (the test date).

The script reads the inventory export, applies the rules in order, writes the sample with the reason of each pick to L1_sample_selected.csv, and prints the coverage: 10 of 45 = 22 %. In the plan, the sample column reads: "10 of 45: 5 judgement (J1 administrator rights, J2 site coverage) + 5 random, seed 20261107". Data are fictional.

L1_sampling_plan.py - Python 3
Code - a comment line explains every code line82 lines
1# TASK: build a reproducible sampling plan that selects 10 of the 45 Windows 11 laptops of
2# Erable Cycles (fictional) for checklist item MC-03 (operating-system patch level).
3# RELATION TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 1 - audit methods and techniques. The script applies
4# judgement-based sampling (risk criteria chosen by the auditor) and then statistical
5# (random) sampling with a fixed seed, and records why every laptop was chosen.
6# FUTURE LABS: Lab 2 Part B step 4 (the "sample" column of your checklist), Lab 3 Part B
7# (patch status, Day 8) and Project section 5 (methodology). Fictional data only.
8
9# Import the csv module, which reads and writes comma-separated values (CSV) files safely.
10import csv
11# Import the random module, which provides a pseudo-random number generator for statistical sampling.
12import random
13
14# Name of the input file: an inventory export of the 45 laptops (population of the test).
15POPULATION_FILE = "L1_laptops_population.csv"
16# Total number of laptops the auditor decided to test (the sample size written in the plan).
17SAMPLE_SIZE = 10
18# Fixed seed (the test date 2026-11-07) so that another auditor re-creates exactly the same random picks.
19SEED = 20261107
20
21# Open the population file in read mode with UTF-8 text encoding.
22with open(POPULATION_FILE, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
23 # Read every row into a dictionary keyed by the header names (laptop_id, site, ...).
24 population = list(csv.DictReader(f))
25# Show how many laptops form the population, to confirm the file is complete.
26print(f"Population: {len(population)} laptops")
27
28# Create an empty dictionary that will map each selected laptop ID to the reason it was chosen.
29selected = {}
30# Judgement criterion J1: laptops with local administrator rights have a higher impact if compromised.
31for row in population:
32 # Keep only the laptops whose local_admin column says "Yes".
33 if row["local_admin"] == "Yes":
34 # Record the laptop with the reason J1 so the choice can be explained in the plan.
35 selected[row["laptop_id"]] = "J1 local administrator rights"
36# Print the laptops chosen by criterion J1.
37print("J1 picks:", ", ".join(selected))
38
39# List the distinct sites (Montreal HQ, Laval store, Quebec City store) present in the population.
40sites = sorted({row["site"] for row in population})
41# Judgement criterion J2: every site must be represented (each type of location is tested).
42for site in sites:
43 # Skip the site if a laptop from it is already in the sample.
44 if any(r["site"] == site and r["laptop_id"] in selected for r in population):
45 # Move on to the next site because this one is already covered.
46 continue
47 # Collect the laptops of this site that are not yet selected.
48 candidates = [r for r in population if r["site"] == site and r["laptop_id"] not in selected]
49 # Choose the laptop with the oldest last security update (highest likelihood of a gap).
50 oldest = min(candidates, key=lambda r: r["last_security_update"])
51 # Record it with the reason J2 and its update date.
52 selected[oldest["laptop_id"]] = f"J2 site coverage, oldest update {oldest['last_security_update']}"
53# Print the judgement-based part of the sample.
54print("Judgement sample:", len(selected), "laptops")
55
56# Create a generator seeded with SEED so the random part is reproducible.
57rng = random.Random(SEED)
58# Build the list of laptops that remain eligible for random selection.
59remaining = [r["laptop_id"] for r in population if r["laptop_id"] not in selected]
60# Draw, without replacement, as many laptops as needed to reach the sample size.
61random_picks = rng.sample(remaining, SAMPLE_SIZE - len(selected))
62# Record each random pick with the reason R and the seed used.
63for lid in sorted(random_picks):
64 # The reason states the method so that the selection can be verified later.
65 selected[lid] = f"R random (seed {SEED})"
66# Print the random picks in ascending order.
67print("Random picks:", ", ".join(sorted(random_picks)))
68
69# Write the final sample to a CSV file that becomes evidence attached to the plan.
70with open("L1_sample_selected.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
71 # Create a writer and write the header line first.
72 writer = csv.writer(f)
73 # The header names the columns that the plan and the Lab 3 test sheet will use.
74 writer.writerow(["laptop_id", "site", "last_security_update", "reason"])
75 # Write one line per selected laptop, in ID order.
76 for row in population:
77 # Only the laptops in the sample are written.
78 if row["laptop_id"] in selected:
79 # Copy the site and the update date from the population, plus the selection reason.
80 writer.writerow([row["laptop_id"], row["site"], row["last_security_update"], selected[row["laptop_id"]]])
81# Print the size of the final sample and the coverage ratio (sample / population).
82print(f"Sample: {len(selected)} of {len(population)} laptops = {len(selected) / len(population):.0%} coverage")
83

    Run it yourself. Save L1_sampling_plan.py and L1_laptops_population.csv in the same folder, then run python3 L1_sampling_plan.py (Windows: py L1_sampling_plan.py). The script writes L1_sample_selected.csv.
    
 
    Step-by-step explanation
    1. The csv module reads the 45 rows of the inventory export into dictionaries; the random module provides the random generator.
    2. J1 loops over the population and keeps the 3 laptops whose local_admin column is Yes; each pick is stored with its reason.
    3. J2 checks every site: Montreal HQ is already represented by a J1 laptop; for Laval and Quebec City the laptop with the oldest update is added (LT-031 and LT-044).
    4. random.Random(20261107) creates a generator whose sequence is always the same for that seed; rng.sample draws 5 of the 40 remaining laptops without replacement.
    5. Every random pick is recorded with the reason 'R random (seed 20261107)', which allows another auditor to repeat the draw.
    6. The script writes the sample to a CSV (comma-separated values) file: this file is evidence attached to the plan and the input list for the Lab 3 patch test.
    7. The last line prints the sample size and the coverage (10 / 45 = 22 %). The same Python version family gives the same random picks for the same seed.

    Q1MCQ - one correct answer
    

    An auditor follows one new-employee request with the IT Administrator, from the HR (Human Resources) form to the creation of the AD (Active Directory) account. Which method is this?
    1. AWalkthrough
      Correct. A walkthrough follows a single real case through every step of the process.
    2. BObservation
      Observation watches an activity as it happens; it does not follow one case through all its steps and documents.
    3. CRe-performance
      Re-performance means the auditor executes the control personally; here the IT (information technology) Administrator performs the steps.
    4. DStatistical sampling
      Only one case is followed, chosen for illustration; no random selection is involved.
    

    

    One real case, from start to end, with the person who performs it.
    Q2MCQ - one correct answer
    

    Why does L1_sampling_plan.py start its random generator with a fixed seed (20261107)?
    1. ASo that anyone running the script again obtains exactly the same random picks
      Correct. A fixed seed makes the pseudo-random sequence reproducible, so the selection can be verified.
    2. BSo that the script runs faster
      The seed has no effect on speed.
    3. CSo that the selected laptops fail the test
      The seed does not influence test results; it only fixes which laptops are drawn.
    4. DSo that the sample becomes judgement-based
      The random part remains statistical; the seed only makes it repeatable.
    

    

    Think about another auditor who must verify the sample.
    Q3MCQ - one correct answer
    

    Which evidence is the most reliable to conclude that Windows Defender Firewall is enabled on LAB-WIN11 today?
    1. AThe output of Get-NetFirewallProfile run by the auditor on LAB-WIN11 today
      Correct. Evidence generated by the system and obtained directly by the auditor at the time of the test is the most reliable.
    2. BThe IT Administrator says it is enabled
      An oral statement alone is the weakest evidence; it must be corroborated.
    3. CThe security policy says firewalls must be enabled
      The policy shows the requirement, not the actual state of the system.
    4. DA screenshot e-mailed by the MSP (managed service provider) last year
      It is old, indirect and could have been modified; it does not show today's state.
    

    

    Who produced the evidence, and when?
    Q4MCQ - one correct answer
    

    In NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-53A Rev. 5, what does the attribute 'coverage' describe?
    1. AWhich and how many objects are assessed (for example how many laptops or accounts)
      Correct. Coverage is the scope of the objects assessed; depth is the rigour of each assessment.
    2. BThe level of detail of an examination or test
      That is depth (basic, focused, comprehensive).
    3. CThe number of auditors in the team
      Coverage concerns the objects assessed, not the team.
    4. DThe frameworks mapped to each control
      Mapping is a crosswalk activity; it is not an assessment attribute.
    

    

    Depth is about rigour; coverage is about something else.
    Q5MSQ - several correct answers (3)
    

    Which statements about judgement-based sampling are correct? (3)
    1. AThe auditor selects items using knowledge of risk
      Correct: the selection is guided by risk, for example administrator laptops.
    2. BIts results cannot be extended statistically to the whole population
      Correct: without known selection probabilities, no statistical estimate is possible.
    3. CThe reason of every pick must be documented
      Correct: the plan records why each item was chosen.
    4. DEvery item has the same chance of being selected
      That describes random (statistical) selection.
    5. EIt requires a random number generator
      Judgement-based selection does not use random draws.
    6. FPCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) forbids it
      PCI DSS v4.x allows sampling that follows the assessor's sampling methodology, provided the sample covers every variant of the population.
    

    

    Three statements describe how the auditor chooses and what can be concluded.
    Q6MSQ - several correct answers (2)
    

    Which situations reduce the reliability of a piece of evidence? (2)
    1. AThe only evidence is an oral statement from the person responsible
      Correct: oral statements must be corroborated.
    2. BA document prepared by the auditee that the auditor cannot verify
      Correct: unverifiable evidence prepared by the assessed party is less reliable.
    3. CA report generated by the system and obtained directly by the auditor
      That increases reliability.
    4. DThe auditor re-performed the check personally
      Re-performance gives strong evidence.
    5. ETwo independent sources give the same result
      Agreement of independent sources strengthens the evidence (corroboration).
    6. FThe auditor kept the original file with its hash
      Keeping the original with a fingerprint protects integrity.
    

    

    Two answers describe indirect or unverified evidence.
    

    

    
 
    2
    Lesson 2 - Selection and application of appropriate tests
    About 10 minutes - course plan topic: Selection and application of appropriate tests
    
 
    
 
    2.1 What a test is 
    

    A test is a defined procedure that compares the actual state of something with an expected result, for one requirement. Before execution, a test has five parts: the requirement (the criterion), the method, the sample, the expected result (the pass rule) and the evidence to keep. After execution, the auditor adds the actual result, the verdict (PASS, FAIL, N/A (not applicable) or Not tested) and the reference of the evidence file. A test is repeatable when another auditor who follows it obtains the same result.
    2.2 Choosing the method from the wording of the requirement 
    

    The verb of the requirement points to the method. "Documented", "approved" or "published" point to document review. "Performed every N months" points to a review of records over a period, usually with sampling. "Configured", "enabled" or "disabled" point to re-performance on the system. "Personnel are aware" points to interviews, corroborated by observation. "Only authorized ports are reachable" points to a reachability test combined with a review of the firewall rules. For an important item, the auditor combines two methods so that the second one corroborates the first.
    

    The requirement says...First methodCorroborate withChecklist example
    

    documented / approvedDocument reviewInterview of the ownerMC-16 Acceptable Use Policy
    

    performed / reviewed every N monthsRecords review + samplingInterviewMC-20 access review
    

    configured / enabledRe-performanceBaseline documentMC-09 host firewall
    

    only approved ports reachableReachability test (Nmap)Firewall-rule reviewMC-19 segmentation
    2.3 Automated and manual tests 
    

    Automated tests (CIS-CAT (CIS Configuration Assessment Tool) Lite, Lynis, PowerShell and Bash scripts) are fast and repeatable, check 100 % of the settings they know, and produce output files that can be fingerprinted. Their limits must be known: a false positive reports a problem that does not exist (for example a setting enforced by another mechanism), a false negative misses a real problem, and every tool has a limited coverage - CIS-CAT Lite assesses Windows 10 and 11 Enterprise, Ubuntu 20.04 and Google Chrome, so Lab 3 uses Lynis for Ubuntu 24.04. Manual tests remain necessary for policies, people and physical controls, and for interpreting tool output.
    2.4 Test of design and test of operating effectiveness 
    

    A test of design checks that a control, as described, would meet the requirement: the Patch Management Procedure requires security updates within 30 days. A test of operating effectiveness checks that the control actually operated over a period: the update history shows a security update every month, each one installed within 30 days. A single screenshot proves that a setting exists at one moment; it does not prove operation over time. Day 9 returns to this distinction.
    2.5 Measurable expected results and evidence handling 
    

    The expected result must be measurable. "Patching is good" cannot be tested. "The newest security update was installed at most 30 days before the test date" can be tested, and it follows PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) requirement 6.3.3 (critical updates within one month). Write the rules for special cases before testing: "N/A (not applicable) - no cardholder data on laptops" and "Not tested - reason" are acceptable entries; an invented result is not.
    

    Evidence is handled with discipline: one naming rule (L3-E07_MC-03_hotfix_LAB-WIN11.csv), the date of collection, a SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) fingerprint that changes if one byte of the file changes (integrity), masking of any real personal information (Legal Notice 6.7 and 18.2), and one line per file in the evidence index. Test once, satisfy many: the same patch report supports CIS (Center for Internet Security) Safeguard 7.3, ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001:2022 control A.8.8, PCI DSS 6.3.3 and NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 PR.PS-02.
    Key terms to learn - Lesson 2
    Test
    A defined procedure that compares an actual state with an expected result for one requirement.
    Expected result (pass rule)
    The measurable condition that makes a test PASS.
    Verdict
    PASS, FAIL, N/A (not applicable, with a reason) or Not tested (with a reason).
    False positive / false negative
    A reported problem that does not exist / a real problem that the test misses.
    Test of design
    Checks that a control, as described, would meet the requirement.
    Test of operating effectiveness
    Checks that a control actually operated over a period.
    SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) fingerprint
    A 64-hexadecimal-character value computed from a file; any change in the file changes the value.
    Test once, satisfy many
    One piece of evidence mapped to several frameworks.
    Think about it
    • Which method would you choose first for 'the Access Control Policy is approved', and how would you corroborate it?
    • Give one example of a false positive from a configuration-assessment tool.

    Real-life example 2
    One complete test: MC-03 patch level on LAB-WIN11
    
 
    TaskRun checklist item MC-03 as a complete test - requirement, method, sample, expected result, evidence - decide PASS or FAIL and keep the evidence with a SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) fingerprint.
    Relation to the lectureShows the five parts of section 2.1, a measurable pass rule (2.5), the difference between existence and operation over time (2.4) and disciplined evidence handling (2.5).
    Future labsLab 2 Part B step 4 (test definitions) and Lab 3 Part B on Day 8 (patch status of both VMs (virtual machines)); Course Procedure Manual chapter 4.
    
 
    The test card states the requirement (security updates within 30 days), the method (re-performance with Get-HotFix, plus a review of the Patch Management Procedure), the sample (LAB-WIN11, all updates) and the pass rule (newest security update at most 30 days old). In class the script reads a fictional export; on your own Windows VM (virtual machine) it reads the real list.
    

    The fictional VM installed an ordinary update on October 28 but its newest security update dates from September 16: 52 days before the test date, so the verdict is FAIL. Only 2 security updates were installed in the last 90 days instead of about 3, which shows that the October monthly update is missing (operating effectiveness). If the script did not filter security updates, the October 28 update (10 days old) would produce a false PASS. The update list is saved as evidence, fingerprinted with SHA-256, and the completed test card is saved as JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) for the Lab 3 findings table.
    
 

    
 
    L2_Test-PatchLevel.ps1 - PowerShell (Windows PowerShell 5.1 or PowerShell 7)
  
  
  
  
  
  
 
    
 
    
  
    Code - a comment line explains every code line63 lines
    1# TASK: run checklist item MC-03 as a complete test - requirement, method, sample, expected
    2#       result and evidence - on the Windows lab VM, then decide PASS or FAIL and keep the
    3#       evidence with a SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) fingerprint.
    4# RELATION TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 2 - selection and application of appropriate tests. The
    5#       expected result is measurable (30 days), the method is re-performance, and the
    6#       evidence file is named, timestamped and hashed.
    7# FUTURE LABS: Lab 2 Part B step 4 (test definition) and Lab 3 Part B, Day 8 (patch status);
    8#       Course Procedure Manual chapter 4. Run it only on your own lab VM (Legal Notice 6.1, 6.4).
    9 
    10# Declare the script parameters: an optional sample CSV, the test date and the maximum age in days.
    11param([string]$SampleCsv = "", [datetime]$TestDate = (Get-Date), [int]$MaxAgeDays = 30)
    12 
    13# Describe the test card: the five parts that make a test repeatable by another auditor.
    14$Test = [ordered]@{ Id = "MC-03"; Requirement = "Security updates installed within $MaxAgeDays days"; Method = "Re-performance (Get-HotFix) + document review"; Sample = "LAB-WIN11 (100 % of updates)"; Expected = "Newest security update <= $MaxAgeDays days old" }
    15# Print the identifier and the requirement so the console output shows which test is running.
    16Write-Host "Test $($Test.Id): $($Test.Requirement)"
    17 
    18# Use the sample file in class (fictional data) or the real update list on your own Windows VM.
    19if ($SampleCsv) {
    20    # Import the fictional export; every field arrives as text.
    21    $Raw = Import-Csv -Path $SampleCsv
    22} else {
    23    # Read the real list of installed updates from Windows (Get-HotFix works only on Windows).
    24    $Raw = Get-HotFix | Select-Object HotFixID, Description, InstalledOn
    25}
    26# Convert every InstalledOn value to a real date so that dates can be compared and subtracted.
    27$Updates = $Raw | ForEach-Object { [pscustomobject]@{ HotFixID = $_.HotFixID; Description = $_.Description; InstalledOn = [datetime]$_.InstalledOn } }
    28# Print how many updates were found in total.
    29Write-Host "Updates found: $($Updates.Count)"
    30 
    31# Keep only the security updates; ordinary updates would hide a missing security patch.
    32$Security = $Updates | Where-Object { $_.Description -match "Security" } | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending
    33# Take the most recent security update (first item after the descending sort).
    34$Newest = $Security | Select-Object -First 1
    35# Compute the age in whole days between the newest security update and the test date.
    36$AgeDays = ($TestDate - $Newest.InstalledOn).Days
    37# Print the newest security update and its age.
    38Write-Host "Newest security update: $($Newest.HotFixID) on $($Newest.InstalledOn.ToString('yyyy-MM-dd')) -> $AgeDays days"
    39 
    40# Count the security updates of the last 90 days: about 3 are expected for a monthly cycle.
    41$Recent = @($Security | Where-Object { $_.InstalledOn -ge $TestDate.AddDays(-90) }).Count
    42# Apply the pass rule written in the plan: newest security update no older than the maximum age.
    43$Result = if ($AgeDays -le $MaxAgeDays) { "PASS" } else { "FAIL" }
    44# Print the operating-effectiveness indicator and the result.
    45Write-Host "Security updates in the last 90 days: $Recent (expected about 3) -> Result: $Result"
    46 
    47# Create the evidence folder if it does not exist yet (-Force makes the command idempotent).
    48New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "evidence" -Force | Out-Null
    49# Build the evidence file name with the course naming rule: lab, evidence number, item, host.
    50$EvidenceFile = Join-Path "evidence" "L3-E07_MC-03_hotfix_LAB-WIN11.csv"
    51# Save the full update list as evidence (all updates, not only the security ones).
    52$Updates | Export-Csv -Path $EvidenceFile -NoTypeInformation
    53# Compute the SHA-256 fingerprint: any later change to the file would change this value.
    54$Hash = (Get-FileHash -Path $EvidenceFile -Algorithm SHA256).Hash
    55# Print the start of the fingerprint (the full value is stored in the test record).
    56Write-Host "Evidence: $EvidenceFile  SHA-256: $($Hash.Substring(0,16))..."
    57 
    58# Add the actual result, the verdict and the evidence details to the test card.
    59$Test.Actual = "$($Newest.HotFixID) installed $AgeDays days before $($TestDate.ToString('yyyy-MM-dd'))"; $Test.Result = $Result; $Test.Evidence = $EvidenceFile; $Test.Sha256 = $Hash
    60# Save the completed test card as JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) next to the evidence file.
    61$Test | ConvertTo-Json | Set-Content -Path "evidence/L3-E07_MC-03_testrecord.json"
    62# Print the final line that will be copied into the findings table of Lab 3.
    63Write-Host "Test record saved: evidence/L3-E07_MC-03_testrecord.json ($Result)"
    64

In class: pwsh -File L2_Test-PatchLevel.ps1 -SampleCsv L2_hotfix_sample.csv -TestDate 2026-11-07 (Windows PowerShell 5.1: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File ... with the same parameters).       Step-by-step explanation
      1. param() declares three inputs: an optional sample CSV (comma-separated values), the test date and the maximum age (30 days).
      2. The ordered hashtable $Test holds the five parts of the test card, so the definition is written before any execution.
      3. In class the script imports the fictional CSV; on a real Windows VM, Get-HotFix reads the installed updates.
      4. The text dates are converted to [datetime] objects so that they can be subtracted.
      5. Where-Object keeps only the security updates; Sort-Object puts the newest first; Select-Object -First 1 takes it.
      6. The age is 52 days; the pass rule (<= 30) gives FAIL; counting the last 90 days (2 updates) shows the missing monthly update.
      7. Export-Csv saves the evidence; Get-FileHash computes its SHA-256 fingerprint; the completed test card is saved as JSON.

      Q1MCQ - one correct answer
      

      Requirement: 'The Acceptable Use Policy is approved and acknowledged by all employees.' Which first method fits best?
      1. ADocument review of the policy, plus a sample of signed acknowledgements
        Correct. Approval is shown by the document; acknowledgement is shown by records, checked on a sample.
      2. BA port-reachability scan of the laptops
        A scan tests network exposure, not policy approval.
      3. CRe-performance with a PowerShell script
        There is no technical setting to execute.
      4. DAn interview with one employee only
        One interview cannot show that all employees acknowledged the policy.
      

      

      The verbs are 'approved' and 'acknowledged by all'.
      Q2MCQ - one correct answer
      

      Without the filter on 'Security', what would the MC-03 example have reported?
      1. AA false PASS, because an ordinary update was installed 10 days before the test date
        Correct. The October 28 update is not a security update; counting it hides the missing security patch.
      2. BThe same FAIL
        The newest update of any kind is only 10 days old, so the rule would pass.
      3. CAn error, because the dates cannot be compared
        The dates are converted to [datetime] and compare correctly.
      4. DN/A (not applicable), because the VM (virtual machine) is a lab machine
        The lab VM is in scope and the requirement applies.
      

      

      Look at the date of the newest update of any kind.
      Q3MCQ - one correct answer
      

      Which expected result is measurable?
      1. AAccounts lock after at most 10 failed attempts for at least 30 minutes
        Correct. Both values can be read from the configuration and compared.
      2. BPasswords are strong
        'Strong' is not defined; two auditors could disagree.
      3. CThe firewall is configured well
        'Well' cannot be verified.
      4. DBackups are done regularly
        'Regularly' needs a period and a success criterion.
      

      

      A measurable rule can be checked as true or false without opinion.
      Q4MCQ - one correct answer
      

      Why does the example compute the SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) value of the evidence file?
      1. ATo show later that the file was not modified after collection
        Correct. Any change to the file would produce a different fingerprint.
      2. BTo encrypt the file
        A hash is not encryption; the file stays readable.
      3. CTo compress the file
        Hashing does not reduce the file size.
      4. DTo remove personal information
        Masking is a separate step; hashing does not alter the content.
      

      

      Think about integrity, not secrecy.
      Q5MSQ - several correct answers (2)
      

      Which statements describe limits of automated assessment tools? (2)
      1. AThey can report false positives that the auditor must analyse
        Correct: tool output needs interpretation.
      2. BThey only cover the platforms and benchmarks they support
        Correct: CIS-CAT (CIS Configuration Assessment Tool) Lite does not assess Ubuntu 24.04, for example.
      3. CThey are always 100 % correct
        Tools produce false positives and false negatives.
      4. DThey replace the need for an assessment plan
        The plan decides what is tested, when, and with which pass rule.
      5. EThey make interviews unnecessary for policies
        Policies and people still need document review and interviews.
      6. FTheir output never needs interpretation
        Interpretation is part of the auditor's work.
      

      

      Two statements describe errors and coverage.
      Q6MSQ - several correct answers (3)
      

      Which elements must a test definition contain BEFORE the test is executed? (3)
      1. AThe requirement (criterion)
        Correct: the test needs its reference.
      2. BThe sample (size and how chosen)
        Correct: the sample is decided in the plan.
      3. CThe expected result (pass rule)
        Correct: the rule is fixed before testing so the verdict is objective.
      4. DThe actual result
        It is recorded after execution.
      5. EThe verdict PASS or FAIL
        It is decided after execution.
      6. FThe auditor's personal opinion of the system
        Opinions are not part of a test definition.
      

      

      Three of the five parts appear below; results come after execution.
      

      

      
 
      3
      Lesson 3 - Development of audit checklists aligned to frameworks
      About 10 minutes - course plan topic: Development of audit checklists aligned to frameworks (e.g., ISO 27001 clauses)
      
 
      
 
      3.1 Why a checklist 
      

      An audit checklist is a working document that lists the items to verify, with the information needed to test each of them. It makes the assessment complete (nothing in scope is forgotten), consistent (every auditor tests the same way), repeatable (next year's audit can compare results) and it plans the evidence in advance. ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 19011 calls such documents work documents; ISO/IEC TS 27008:2019 gives guidance on reviewing and assessing information security controls. A checklist does not replace judgement: when the auditor notices a problem outside the list, it is recorded as an observation.
      3.2 Anatomy of a checklist line 
      

      Each line of the course checklist has the same fields: ID and item name; type (C configuration, T technical control, A administrative control, S segmentation or access); the framework references - CIS (Center for Internet Security) Controls v8.1 Safeguard with its Implementation Group, ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001:2022 Annex A control, PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) v4.0.1 requirement, NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 subcategory; the requirement in our own words; the test procedure; the method; the sample; the expected result; the expected evidence; and, after testing, the result and notes.
      3.3 Aligning with frameworks: the crosswalk 
      

      A crosswalk (or mapping) links one requirement of a framework to the equivalent requirements of other frameworks. One checklist line with four references lets one test serve four frameworks. CIS (Center for Internet Security) publishes mappings between the CIS Controls, NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 and ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001; tools such as CIS CSAT (free) and CISO Assistant (open source) manage checklists with mappings.
      

      Not every item maps to every framework. MC-11 (disk encryption on laptops) has no PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) reference because no cardholder data is stored on the laptops; writing "-" is more accurate than forcing a mapping. The ISO/IEC 27001 text is licensed: the checklist cites the control number and states the requirement in our own words (Legal Notice 7.5).
      3.4 The course Master Checklist (20 items) 
      

      The Master Checklist gives 20 ready-made lines: 8 configuration items (MC-01 to MC-08) tested in Lab 3 Parts A-B with tools and scripts, 7 technical controls (MC-09 to MC-15), 3 administrative controls (MC-16 to MC-18) and 2 segmentation and access items (MC-19, MC-20) verified in Lab 3 Part C. Every item states its assets: the critical assets of the case and the two VMs (virtual machines), which stand in for the production systems of the same platform.
      3.5 Five selection rules and coverage 
      

      Lab 2 Part B selects 12 to 15 items with five written rules: (1) the item tests at least one in-scope asset; (2) items driven by a legal or contractual requirement from Lab 1 are included (MC-12, MC-18, MC-19, MC-20); (3) every platform in scope gets its secure-baseline item (MC-01 Windows, MC-02 Linux, MC-08 cloud - CIS (Center for Internet Security) Safeguard 4.1, PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) 2.2.1); (4) every in-scope asset is tested at least once; (5) the checklist keeps at least 3 configuration and 3 control items. Remaining places are filled by priority: 2 points per critical asset covered, 1 point per VM (virtual machine).
      

      Coverage is then measured: references per framework and tests per asset. In the example, DB-RDS01 (A04), the firewall (A07) and the payment provider (A10) are each tested by a single item - acceptable, but an auditor may add MC-14 or MC-15 to test the database more deeply.
      Key terms to learn - Lesson 3
      Audit checklist
      A working document listing the items to verify, with references, test procedure and expected evidence.
      Crosswalk (mapping)
      A table linking a requirement of one framework to equivalent requirements of others.
      Implementation Group (IG)
      CIS (Center for Internet Security) prioritization of Safeguards: IG1 (56 essential Safeguards), IG2 (Implementation Group 2), IG3.
      Configuration item (C)
      A checklist item that compares settings with a baseline (Lab 3 Parts A-B).
      Control item (T, A, S)
      A checklist item that verifies a technical, administrative or segmentation/access control (Lab 3 Part C).
      Stand-in
      A lab VM (virtual machine) tested in place of a production system of the same platform.
      Coverage (checklist)
      How many items test each asset and how many lines carry each framework's reference.
      Think about it
      • Why is it better to write '-' in the PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) column of MC-11 than to force a reference?
      • Which in-scope asset is tested by only one item in the example, and what would you add?

      Real-life example 3
      Building the Lab 2 Part B checklist with written rules
      
 
      TaskSelect 12-15 items from the 20-item Master Checklist with five written rules, then measure coverage per framework and per asset.
      Relation to the lectureApplies the checklist anatomy (3.2), the crosswalk (3.3) and the selection rules (3.5) to the Erable Cycles scope.
      Future labsLab 2 Part B step 3 (your checklist), Lab 3 Parts A-C (the items you test) and Project section 5. The output file feeds the Lesson 5 scheduling example.
      
 
      The script reads the Master Checklist and the scope written in Lab 2 Part A (the 5 critical assets and the 2 VMs (virtual machines)). All 20 items touch an in-scope asset (rule 1). Rule 2 adds the four legal or contractual items, MC-12, MC-18, MC-19 and MC-20. Rule 3 adds one secure baseline per platform found in the scope: MC-01 (Windows), MC-02 (Linux) and MC-08 (cloud). Rule 4 finds that every asset is already covered. Rule 5 fills the checklist to 14 items by priority (MC-03, MC-06, MC-07, then MC-04, MC-05, MC-09, MC-13).
      

      The balance is 8 configuration and 6 control items (rule 6 check), every line carries references for the four frameworks, and the file Lab2B_audit_checklist.csv is written with semicolons because the references themselves contain commas.
      
 

      
 
      L3_build_checklist.py - Python 3
  
  
  
  
  
  
 
      
 
      
  
      Code - a comment line explains every code line115 lines
      1# TASK: build the Lab 2 Part B audit checklist by selecting 12-15 items from the 20-item
      2#       Master Checklist, following written selection rules, and measure its coverage of the
      3#       in-scope assets and of the four frameworks (CIS v8.1, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, PCI DSS
      4#       v4.0.1, NIST CSF 2.0).
      5# RELATION TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 3 - development of audit checklists aligned to frameworks.
      6#       Every selected line keeps its framework references (a crosswalk), and the rules
      7#       guarantee at least 3 configuration items and 3 control items.
      8# FUTURE LABS: Lab 2 Part B step 3 (your checklist), Lab 3 Parts A-C (the items you test),
      9#       Project section 5. The output file feeds the scheduling example of Lesson 5.
      10 
      11# Import the csv module to read the Master Checklist and the scope, and to write the result.
      12import csv
      13 
      14# Number of items the auditor wants in the final checklist (the plan allows 12 to 15).
      15TARGET = 14
      16# Item types that count as "controls" (technical, administrative, segmentation / access).
      17CONTROL_TYPES = {"T", "A", "S"}
      18 
      19# Read the 20 Master Checklist items into a list of dictionaries.
      20with open("L3_master_checklist.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
      21    # Each row becomes a dictionary keyed by the column names (id, title, type, ...).
      22    master = list(csv.DictReader(f))
      23# Read the scope written in Lab 2 Part A: the 5 critical assets and the 2 lab VMs.
      24with open("L3_scope.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
      25    # Keep the scope rows in a list as well.
      26    scope_rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
      27# Build the set of in-scope asset IDs for quick membership tests.
      28scope = {r["asset_id"] for r in scope_rows}
      29# Build the subset of critical assets (critical column = yes).
      30critical = {r["asset_id"] for r in scope_rows if r["critical"] == "yes"}
      31# Turn the asset field "A01|V01" of every item into a Python set.
      32for item in master:
      33    # Splitting on the vertical bar gives the list of assets the item can be tested on.
      34    item["asset_set"] = set(item["assets"].split("|"))
      35 
      36# Rule 1: keep only the items that apply to at least one in-scope asset (or to the whole company).
      37eligible = [m for m in master if m["asset_set"] & scope or "ALL" in m["asset_set"]]
      38# Print how many items survive rule 1.
      39print(f"Rule 1 - eligible items: {len(eligible)} of {len(master)}")
      40 
      41# Priority score: 2 points per critical asset covered, 1 point per lab VM covered.
      42def priority(item):
      43    # Count the critical assets and the VMs that this item covers, then weight them.
      44    return 2 * len(item["asset_set"] & critical) + len(item["asset_set"] & (scope - critical))
      45 
      46# Rule 2: items driven by a legal or contractual requirement from Lab 1 are always included.
      47selected = [m for m in eligible if m["legal"] == "yes"]
      48# Print the identifiers of the mandatory items.
      49print("Rule 2 - legal / contractual items:", ", ".join(m["id"] for m in selected))
      50 
      51# Collect the platforms present in the scope (Windows, Linux, Cloud, ...); "Linux|Cloud" gives two.
      52platforms = {p for r in scope_rows for p in r["platform"].split("|")}
      53# Rule 3: every in-scope platform gets its secure-baseline item (CIS Safeguard 4.1, PCI DSS 2.2.1).
      54for item in eligible:
      55    # The baseline_for column names the platform whose baseline the item checks (empty otherwise).
      56    if item["baseline_for"] in platforms and item not in selected:
      57        # Add the baseline item; Lab 3 Part A runs these checks with CIS-CAT Lite, Lynis or cloud tools.
      58        selected.append(item)
      59# Print the checklist size after the two mandatory rules.
      60print("Rule 3 - platform baselines added; checklist now has", len(selected), "items")
      61 
      62# Rule 4: every in-scope asset must be covered by at least one selected item.
      63for asset in sorted(scope):
      64    # Skip the asset if an already-selected item covers it.
      65    if any(asset in m["asset_set"] for m in selected):
      66        # Nothing to add for this asset.
      67        continue
      68    # Among the remaining eligible items that cover the asset, take the one with the highest priority.
      69    best = max((m for m in eligible if asset in m["asset_set"] and m not in selected), key=priority)
      70    # Add it to the checklist.
      71    selected.append(best)
      72    # Print which item was added to cover which asset.
      73    print(f"Rule 4 - {asset} covered by {best['id']}")
      74 
      75# Rule 5: fill up to the target size with the highest-priority remaining items (ties: lowest ID).
      76for item in sorted(eligible, key=lambda m: (-priority(m), m["id"])):
      77    # Stop when the checklist reaches the target size.
      78    if len(selected) >= TARGET:
      79        # Leave the loop.
      80        break
      81    # Add the item only if it is not already in the checklist.
      82    if item not in selected:
      83        # Append the item to the checklist.
      84        selected.append(item)
      85 
      86# Rule 6: check the balance required by the plan (at least 3 configuration and 3 control items).
      87n_config = sum(1 for m in selected if m["type"] == "C")
      88# Count the control items (types T, A and S).
      89n_control = sum(1 for m in selected if m["type"] in CONTROL_TYPES)
      90# Print the balance and whether the rule is met.
      91print(f"Rule 6 - configuration: {n_config}, controls: {n_control} ->", "OK" if n_config >= 3 and n_control >= 3 else "NOT MET")
      92 
      93# Sort the final checklist by item ID so that it is easy to read and cite.
      94selected.sort(key=lambda m: m["id"])
      95# Measure coverage: for each framework, count the items that carry a reference ("-" means none).
      96for fw in ["cis", "iso", "pci", "csf"]:
      97    # A reference counts when the field is not empty and does not start with "-".
      98    covered = sum(1 for m in selected if m[fw] and not m[fw].startswith("-"))
      99    # Print the number of referenced items for this framework.
      100    print(f"Coverage {fw.upper()}: {covered}/{len(selected)} items")
      101# Print the in-scope assets and the number of items that will test each of them.
      102print("Items per asset:", ", ".join(f"{a}={sum(1 for m in selected if a in m['asset_set'])}" for a in sorted(scope)))
      103 
      104# Write the checklist with a semicolon delimiter (references already contain commas).
      105with open("Lab2B_audit_checklist.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
      106    # Create a writer that separates fields with semicolons.
      107    writer = csv.writer(f, delimiter=";")
      108    # Write the header of the checklist file.
      109    writer.writerow(["id", "title", "type", "cis", "iso", "pci", "csf", "assets", "lab3"])
      110    # Write one line per selected item.
      111    for m in selected:
      112        # Copy the columns needed by the plan and by the scheduling script.
      113        writer.writerow([m["id"], m["title"], m["type"], m["cis"], m["iso"], m["pci"], m["csf"], m["assets"], m["lab3"]])
      114# Print the final size of the checklist.
      115print(f"Checklist written: {len(selected)} items -> Lab2B_audit_checklist.csv")
      116

        Step-by-step explanation
        1. TARGET and CONTROL_TYPES hold the two numbers of the plan: 14 items, and the types that count as controls.
        2. The Master Checklist and the scope are read with csv.DictReader; the asset field of each item becomes a set.
        3. Rule 1 keeps items that touch an in-scope asset; rule 2 adds the legal and contractual items.
        4. Rule 3 reads the platform column of the scope (Windows, Linux, Cloud) and adds the matching baseline items.
        5. Rule 4 checks every asset; rule 5 sorts the remaining items by priority and adds them until 14 items are reached.
        6. The balance check counts 8 configuration and 6 control items; the coverage loop counts references per framework.
        7. The checklist is written with a semicolon delimiter for the Bash script of Lesson 5.

        4
        Lesson 4 - Risk analysis fundamentals for assessing impact and likelihood
        About 10 minutes - course plan topic: Risk analysis fundamentals for assessing impact and likelihood
        
 
        
 
        4.1 Risk vocabulary 
        

        ISO 31000:2018 defines risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives. In information security practice, a risk is described by an event and expressed as the combination of its likelihood (how probable the event is) and its impact (also called consequence: what the event does to the organization). The event happens when a threat (a potential cause of an incident, for example an attacker or a hardware failure) exploits a vulnerability (a weakness of an asset or of a control) of an asset from your inventory.
        

        A control is a measure that modifies risk. Inherent risk is the risk before the controls are considered; residual risk is the risk that remains after the controls or the treatment. A compensating control is a different control that reduces the same risk when the expected control is missing: for example, a firewall rule that limits SSH (Secure Shell) to the administration subnet reduces the likelihood of attacks on a server whose SSH configuration is weak.
        4.2 Qualitative, semi-quantitative and quantitative analysis 
        

        A qualitative analysis uses ordered levels (Low, Medium, High) defined in words. A semi-quantitative analysis gives numbers to those levels (1, 2, 3) and combines them, usually by multiplication. A quantitative analysis expresses risk in money. The three classic formulas are: SLE (single loss expectancy) = asset value x exposure factor (the fraction of the value lost in one event); ARO (annualized rate of occurrence) = the expected number of events per year; ALE (annualized loss expectancy) = SLE x ARO.
        

        Fictional example: one day of online sales of Erable Cycles is worth $12,000; an outage of WEB-APP01 loses half a day, so the exposure factor is 0.5 and the SLE is $6,000. If such an outage is expected once every two years (ARO = 0.5), the ALE is $3,000 per year. A control that removes most of this risk is economically justified if it costs less than $3,000 per year. Quantitative values need reliable data, which small organizations rarely have; this course therefore uses a semi-quantitative 3x3 matrix. NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 uses five levels (Very Low to Very High) and describes the same three approaches.
        4.3 The course 3x3 matrix and its one-line scales 
        

        The course matrix multiplies a likelihood level (1 to 3) by an impact level (1 to 3). The score-to-level rule converts the product into a risk level: 1-2 = Low, 3-4 = Medium, 6 = High, 9 = Critical. Each level of each scale has a one-line definition, so that two auditors who read the same finding choose the same level.
        

        LevelLikelihood - one-line definitionImpact - one-line definition
        

        1 LowNeeds physical access or several unlikely conditions together, or a strong compensating control exists.Inconvenience only; no legal duty affected (Day 4 impact criteria).
        

        2 MediumNeeds internal network access or a specific condition, or only a partial compensating control exists.A process degraded for more than one day with a workaround, or internal data exposed.
        

        3 HighReachable from the Internet or by any employee, already observed or exploited, and no compensating control.A legal duty breached (PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act), Law 25, PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)) or a High-impact process stopped.
        

        The impact scale reuses the business-impact criteria of Day 4, so the inventory and the risk analysis stay consistent: a finding on a Restricted asset with the PI (personal information) or CHD (cardholder data) flag usually reaches impact 3.
        4.4 Rating a finding: four elements and five steps 
        

        A finding is rated only when it is well described. The four elements used in audit reports are the condition (what the auditor observed), the criterion (the requirement), the cause (why the gap exists) and the effect (what can happen). The rating then follows five steps: (1) identify the asset and its business impact in the inventory; (2) choose the likelihood with the scale, taking exposure and compensating controls into account; (3) choose the impact with the scale; (4) compute the score and the level; (5) write a one-sentence justification that quotes the scale definitions.
        

        Calibration is the exercise in which several auditors rate the same findings and compare their ratings; differences show where a definition is unclear. When two findings have the same score, the course rule places first the finding that has a legal or contractual deadline.
        4.5 Where risk is used: before, during and after testing 
        

        Before testing, risk decides the priorities of the plan: items that touch critical assets are tested first and with more depth and coverage (risk-based audit planning). During and after testing, every nonconformity receives a rating, and the rating orders the findings table of Lab 3 and the recommendations of the Project (section 7). ISO/IEC 27005:2022 names four risk treatment options: risk modification (add or improve controls), risk retention (accept the risk with a documented decision), risk avoidance (stop the activity) and risk sharing (for example insurance or a contract with a provider). The free CIS RAM applies the same logic to the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Controls.
        

        The auditor rates and reports risks; the decision to treat or accept a risk belongs to the risk owner, usually the asset owner identified on Day 4.
        Key terms to learn - Lesson 4
        Risk
        Effect of uncertainty on objectives, as defined in ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 31000; in practice, likelihood x impact of an event.
        Likelihood
        How probable the event is, considering exposure and existing controls.
        Impact (consequence)
        What the event does to the organization: legal, operational, financial.
        Threat / vulnerability
        A potential cause of an incident / a weakness that a threat can exploit.
        Inherent / residual risk
        Risk before controls / risk remaining after controls or treatment.
        Compensating control
        A different control that reduces the same risk when the expected control is missing.
        SLE (single loss expectancy), ARO (annualized rate of occurrence), ALE (annualized loss expectancy)
        Single loss expectancy = asset value x exposure factor; annualized rate of occurrence; annualized loss expectancy = SLE x ARO.
        Score-to-level rule
        1-2 Low, 3-4 Medium, 6 High, 9 Critical.
        Calibration
        Several auditors rate the same findings and compare, to remove ambiguity in the scales.
        Risk treatment options
        Modification, retention, avoidance, sharing (ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005:2022).
        Think about it
        • SSH (Secure Shell) root login is allowed on the web-server stand-in, but a firewall rule limits SSH to the administration subnet. How does this change the likelihood?
        • Why does the impact scale reuse the Day 4 business-impact criteria?

        TaskRate seven practice findings (F1-F7) with the course matrix, sort them by score and legal deadline, and print the distribution of levels.

        The page contains seven findings taken from typical Lab 3 results. Each has a likelihood and an impact chosen with the one-line scales. F1 (SSH (Secure Shell) root login allowed on the WEB-APP01 stand-in) is reachable from the Internet and touches the online store: 3 x 3 = 9, Critical. F2 (two accounts inactive for more than 90 days) and F3 (RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) reachable from the office VLAN (virtual local area network) to the domain controller) need internal access but touch Restricted assets: 2 x 3 = 6, High.         L4_risk_calibration.html - HTML + JavaScript (any browser)
  
  
  
  
  
  
 
        
 
        
  
        Code - a comment line explains every code line71 lines
        1<!-- The DOCTYPE line below tells the browser to use the HTML5 standards mode. -->
        2<!DOCTYPE html>
        3<!-- TASK: rate seven practice findings with the course 3x3 matrix (likelihood x impact),
        4     convert each score into a level, rank the findings and flag legal deadlines.
        5     RELATION TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 4 - risk analysis fundamentals for assessing impact and
        6     likelihood. The findings are invented only to calibrate the scales before Lab 3.
        7     FUTURE LABS: Lab 2 Part B step 5 (risk method), Project section 7 (rating of the 8-10
        8     non-conformities) and the 30-60-90 corrective-action plan (Day 10). -->
        9<!-- The html element holds the whole page; lang="en" declares English for screen readers. -->
        10<html lang="en">
        11<!-- The head holds information about the page that is not displayed in the body. -->
        12<head>
        13<!-- UTF-8 encoding lets accented characters (Erable, Quebec) display correctly. -->
        14<meta charset="utf-8">
        15<!-- Title shown in the browser tab. -->
        16<title>L4 Risk calibration - 3x3 matrix</title>
        17<!-- Minimal styles: bordered cells and one background colour per risk level. -->
        18<style>td,th{border:1px solid #94a3b8;padding:4px 8px}.Low{background:#bbf7d0}.Medium{background:#fef08a}.High{background:#fed7aa}.Critical{background:#fecaca}</style>
        19<!-- End of the head. -->
        20</head>
        21<!-- The body contains everything the reader sees. -->
        22<body>
        23<!-- Heading that states what the page shows. -->
        24<h1>Risk calibration on the 3x3 matrix (practice findings)</h1>
        25<!-- Table with a header row; the script below adds one row per finding. -->
        26<table id="out"><tr><th>Rank</th><th>Finding</th><th>L</th><th>I</th><th>Score</th><th>Level</th><th>Legal deadline</th></tr></table>
        27<!-- The script runs when the browser reaches it, after the table exists. -->
        28<script>
        29// Practice findings: id, checklist item, text, likelihood L (1-3), impact I (1-3), legal deadline flag.
        30const findings = [
        31  // F1: a configuration weakness reachable from the Internet on a critical server.
        32  {id: "F1", item: "MC-07", text: "SSH root login allowed on the WEB-APP01 stand-in", L: 3, I: 3, legal: false},
        33  // F2: dormant accounts can still open systems that hold personal information.
        34  {id: "F2", item: "MC-20", text: "Two accounts inactive for more than 90 days", L: 2, I: 3, legal: false},
        35  // F3: a segmentation gap between the office VLAN and the domain controller.
        36  {id: "F3", item: "MC-19", text: "RDP 3389 reachable from the office VLAN to SRV-DC01", L: 2, I: 3, legal: false},
        37  // F4: anti-malware signatures out of date on one sampled laptop.
        38  {id: "F4", item: "MC-10", text: "Defender signatures 9 days old on a sampled laptop", L: 2, I: 2, legal: false},
        39  // F5: a policy that exists only as a draft cannot be enforced.
        40  {id: "F5", item: "MC-17", text: "Access Control Policy still a draft", L: 2, I: 2, legal: false},
        41  // F6: a contractual deadline (PCI DSS 12.8.4: provider status checked every 12 months).
        42  {id: "F6", item: "MC-18", text: "Payment provider AOC older than 12 months", L: 1, I: 3, legal: true},
        43  // F7: the lab VM holds no business data, so the impact is low.
        44  {id: "F7", item: "MC-11", text: "BitLocker off on the lab VM (no business data)", L: 1, I: 1, legal: false},
        45];
        46// Convert a score into a level with the rule of the plan: 1-2 Low, 3-4 Medium, 6 High, 9 Critical.
        47function level(score) { return score <= 2 ? "Low" : score <= 4 ? "Medium" : score <= 6 ? "High" : "Critical"; }
        48// Compute the score (likelihood multiplied by impact) and the level of every finding.
        49for (const f of findings) { f.score = f.L * f.I; f.level = level(f.score); }
        50// Sort: highest score first; equal scores -> legal deadline first; then by identifier.
        51findings.sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score || (b.legal - a.legal) || a.id.localeCompare(b.id));
        52// Get the table element that receives the result rows.
        53const table = document.getElementById("out");
        54// Add one row per finding, in priority order.
        55findings.forEach((f, i) => {
        56  // Insert a new empty row at the end of the table.
        57  const row = table.insertRow();
        58  // Fill the cells: rank, finding, L, I, score, coloured level, legal flag.
        59  row.innerHTML = `<td>${i + 1}</td><td>${f.id} (${f.item}) ${f.text}</td><td>${f.L}</td><td>${f.I}</td><td>${f.score}</td><td class="${f.level}">${f.level}</td><td>${f.legal ? "Yes - plan first" : ""}</td>`;
        60  // Write the same line to the browser console (open it with F12).
        61  console.log(`${i + 1}. ${f.id} ${f.level} (${f.L}x${f.I}=${f.score})${f.legal ? " legal deadline" : ""}`);
        62});
        63// Count the findings per level to summarize the calibration.
        64const counts = findings.reduce((acc, f) => { acc[f.level] = (acc[f.level] || 0) + 1; return acc; }, {});
        65// Print the summary line in the console.
        66console.log("Summary: " + JSON.stringify(counts));
        67</script>
        68<!-- End of the body. -->
        69</body>
        70<!-- End of the document. -->
        71</html>
        72

          5
          Lesson 5 - Scheduling and planning compliance assessment activities
          About 10 minutes - course plan topic: Scheduling and planning compliance assessment activities
          
 
          
 
          5.1 Audit programme and audit plan 
          

          ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 19011 distinguishes two levels of planning. An audit programme is the set of arrangements for one or more audits planned for a specific period and directed toward a specific purpose - for example, the yearly programme of Erable Cycles: access control in the first quarter, backups in the second, PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) readiness before the holiday season. An audit plan describes the activities and arrangements of one audit: what is assessed, how, by whom, where and when. Your Lab 2 Part B deliverable is an audit plan for the assessment that you will conduct in Lab 3.
          

          ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.2.2 asks an organization to plan and maintain an internal audit programme (frequency, methods, responsibilities, planning requirements and reporting), to consider the importance of the processes and the results of previous audits, to define the criteria and scope of each audit, to choose auditors who are objective and impartial, and to report the results to management (paraphrase; the text of the standard is licensed).
          5.2 What an audit plan contains 
          

          An audit plan states the objectives (what the assessment must determine), the scope (assets, locations, processes and period), the criteria (the requirements of Lab 1), the methods and samples, the schedule (dates, times and places of each activity), the roles (auditor, auditee contacts, technical guide), the resources (tools, accounts, lab VMs (virtual machines)), the communication rules, the format of the report and the confidentiality rules. The level of detail depends on the size of the audit: a plan for two lab VMs and five critical assets fits in four to five pages.
          

          Lab 2 Part B sectionContentsFeeds the Project
          

          1 Scope and objectives5 critical assets + 2 VMs in scope; out-of-scope assets with a reason; requirements; periodSection 2
          

          2 Mandate and authorizationLetter adapted from Annex D: systems, activities, exclusions, period, contact, signature, dateSection 2
          

          3 Audit checklist12-15 items, mapped to four frameworksSection 5
          

          4 Tests, samples, evidenceMethod, sample, pass rule, evidence file name per itemSection 5
          

          5 Risk method3x3 matrix, one-line scales, score-to-level ruleSections 5 and 7
          

          6 Schedule, tools, meetingsDays 7-10, tools, roles, constraints, meeting agendasSection 5
          5.3 The mandate comes before any test 
          

          A mandate is the written authorization, given by the person who has the authority over the systems (the asset owner or the chief executive), that defines what the assessor may do, on which systems, during which period, and what is excluded. Section 6.1 of the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice requires written authorization before any monitoring, scanning or testing, and its Annex D provides the template that Lab 2 adapts. Without authorization, accessing a computer system can be a criminal offence in Canada (Criminal Code, s. 342.1).
          

          ISO/IEC 27002:2022 control 8.34 (protection of information systems during audit testing) gives practical rules: agree audit tests and access with management, limit technical tests to read-only access whenever possible, run tests that may affect availability outside business hours, and monitor and log the access of auditors. NIST SP 800-115 provides a rules of engagement template for technical tests.
          5.4 Constraints and dependencies 
          

          The schedule respects four kinds of constraints. Business constraints: the stores and the head office are open 09:00-18:00 Monday to Saturday, so a network scan that may slow the systems runs after 18:00. Change freeze: from November 20 to November 30 (Black Friday on November 27, Cyber Monday on November 30), no change and no intrusive test is allowed. Dependencies: the baseline tools of Lab 3 Part A run first, the check scripts of Part B second, the controls of Part C last, because Part C reuses the results of Parts A and B. Preconditions: the mandate is signed and both VMs (virtual machines) have a snapshot before the first test (Legal Notice 6.4).
          

          DayDateLab blockPlanned activity
          

          Day 7Wed Nov 1119:45-22:00Kick-off meeting; Lab 3 Part A - baseline tools (CIS-CAT (CIS Configuration Assessment Tool) Lite, Policy Analyzer, Lynis)
          

          Day 8Sat Nov 1409:45-13:30Lab 3 Part B - check scripts, patch status, findings table
          

          Day 9Tue Nov 1719:45-22:00Lab 3 Part C - controls, segmentation scan, access review
          

          Day 10Wed Nov 18eveningLab 3 finish; closing meeting; Project kick-off
          5.5 Opening and closing meetings 
          

          The opening meeting (kick-off) takes place before the first test. Its purpose, as described in ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 19011, is to confirm that all participants agree with the audit plan, to introduce the audit team and their roles, and to make sure that all planned activities can be performed. In the plan, its agenda has three bullets: confirm scope, objectives and schedule; confirm the mandate, the constraints and the contacts; agree how evidence and preliminary findings are communicated.
          

          The closing meeting takes place after the tests. The auditor presents the findings and the preliminary conclusions, confirms that the auditee understands them, and explains the next steps (report, corrective actions, follow-up). Its agenda also has three bullets: present the findings with their ratings; confirm facts and note disagreements; agree on the date of the report and of the corrective-action plan.
          Key terms to learn - Lesson 5
          Audit programme
          Arrangements for one or more audits over a period, toward a specific purpose (ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 19011).
          Audit plan
          Description of the activities and arrangements of one audit.
          Mandate (authorization)
          Written permission from the system owner defining systems, activities, exclusions, period and contact.
          Rules of engagement
          The agreed conditions of technical testing (NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-115 template).
          Change freeze
          A period in which no change and no intrusive test is allowed (Nov 20-30 for the case).
          Opening meeting
          Meeting before the tests to confirm the plan, the team, the mandate and the logistics.
          Closing meeting
          Meeting after the tests to present findings and agree on next steps.
          Think about it
          • Why must the segmentation scan (MC-19) run after 18:00 and before November 20?
          • Who should sign the mandate for the Erable Cycles systems, and why not the IT (information technology) Administrator alone?
